title: Add RAG decision-tree stubkit and non-blocking tool-caller quickstart
author: Jordan Patel
description: Context: This quickstart introduces a compact 'decision-tree stubkit' pattern for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) authoring where control flow is expressed as an explicit, testable decision tree and tool calls are executed in a non-blocking manner (awaitable tool futures). Motivation: Many of our RAG quickstarts assume linear or agent-style planning; teams building deterministic orchestration layers wanted a lightweight, auditable alternative that combines explicit branching with tool-calling concurrency to improve throughput and deterministic testability. What this PR adds: a) a minimal starter repository under quickstarts/decision-tree-stubkit with TypeScript and Python runners that show the pattern; b) a compact decision-tree spec (YAML schema) and a TypeScript compiler that emits runtime-ready JSON trees; c) a non-blocking tool-caller wrapper used in examples that runs I/O-bound tools (HTTP lookups, vector DB reads, external enrichment) as Promise/async tasks and aggregates results into the tree context; d) docs site updates (quickstarts index and step-by-step tutorial), a small e2e smoke test, and telemetry probes for tracing branch decisions (trace keys emitted via existing telemetry helper). The description below includes a short usage guide, dev checklist and compatibility notes. Usage: clone quickstarts/decision-tree-stubkit, run `yarn install && yarn start` for the TypeScript sample or `pip install -r requirements.txt && python runner.py` for the Python runner. The TypeScript runner ships with a sample decision-tree YAML (examples/basic-tree.yaml) that demonstrates: 1) fetch candidate docs (non-blocking tool), 2) evaluate recall threshold (synchronous predicate node), 3) fork to a clarification tool or generation step (concurrent enrichment). The provided tool-caller exposes a small interface: registerTool(name, fn) and invokeTool(name, args) returning a future/promise-like token which can be awaited at later nodes. Checklist: - [x] Quickstart code (TS + Py) committed - [x] YAML spec + schema tests - [x] Docs tutorial and quickstarts index entry - [x] smoke e2e test in CI - [x] telemetry probes added - [x] license and readme updates Compatibility notes: uses existing Redwood SDK client for ephemeral API keys and the open model adaptor; works with hosted Redwood API and local emulators. Not a breaking change; isolated under quickstarts. Commits summary: "add initial decision-tree stubkit sample", "add non-blocking tool-caller implementation (ts/py)", "yaml spec and schema validation", "docs quickstart tutorial and smoke test", "fix telemetry keys and update README". Files changed (high level): quickstarts/decision-tree-stubkit/{README.md, examples/basic-tree.yaml, ts-runner/*, py-runner/*, schema/tree-schema.yaml}, docs/quickstarts.md (index add), ci/smoke-quickstarts.yml, telemetry/probes/decision-tree.json. Review conversation summary: Evan requested clearer naming between "task" and "tool" which was addressed by renaming registerTool->registerExternalTool in TS and adding inline comments. Lina requested an example of partial failure handling for tool futures; author added a small retry+fallback example in ts-runner/tools/http_lookup.ts and documented the fallback policy. Priya asked for stricter schema validation and unit tests; added ajv-based tests for TS and pydantic checks for Python. CI notes: initial lint run failed on max-line-length in README; subsequent run passed. e2e smoke test runs in the quickstart CI matrix and passed on Node 18 and Python 3.11. Merge notes: squashed and merged after approvals from Lina and Priya, changelog entry added to quickstarts release notes. Related: ENG-12829 tracks a follow-up to wire the telemetry into consoles, PM-4432 is the product brief for decision-tree UX. Impact and follow-ups: we expect this pattern to be useful for teams wanting deterministic branching, and it provides a clear migration path for agent-style orchestration to become testable. Follow-ups: add a Go runner, create a real-world sample that wires to a customer vector DB adapter, and add a tutorial video.
